description: Curated thoracic radiology evidence corpus for LungRay LangGraph Corrective RAG (CRAG). All 16 pathologies decomposed into 48 atomic chunks (3 facets per pathology) with authoritative guideline citations.

guidelines.FLEISCHNER: Fleischner Society Glossary of Terms for Thoracic Imaging (2024), terminology: https://doi.org/10.1148/radiol.232558
guidelines.TB_WHO: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 3: diagnosis (2025): https://tbksp.who.int/sites/default/files/2025-08/9789240110991-eng.pdf
guidelines.COVID_WHO: WHO guidelines on the use of chest imaging in COVID-19 (2022): https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240055704
guidelines.BTS_PLEURAL: British Thoracic Society Guideline for Pleural Disease (2023): https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784

coding_note_default: Candidate ICD-10 reference category only; requires physician confirmation. A16.2 applies to bacteriologically unconfirmed pulmonary TB; U07.1 requires viral confirmation; Hernia requires anatomical subtype confirmation.

diseases.hallmarks: Increased parenchymal opacity accompanied by regional volume loss, interlobar fissure displacement, ipsilateral hemidiaphragm elevation, or mediastinal shift toward the affected side.
diseases.differential: Lobar consolidation without volume loss, pleural effusion (causes contralateral mediastinal shift), and subpulmonic fluid collection.
diseases.followup: Correlate with prior radiographs and clinical airway status; consider contrast-enhanced chest CT if lobar collapse persists or endobronchial obstruction is suspected.

diseases.hallmarks: Enlarged cardiac silhouette with cardiothoracic ratio > 0.50 on an upright posteroanterior (PA) chest radiograph; anteroposterior (AP) projection and poor inspiration can cause geometric pseudo-cardiomegaly.
diseases.differential: AP projection magnification, pericardial effusion (water-bottle configuration), anterior mediastinal mass, and pectus excavatum.
diseases.followup: Verify radiographic projection (PA vs AP) and inspiratory effort; clinician may consider transthoracic echocardiography and BNP correlation when heart failure or pericardial disease is suspected.

diseases.hallmarks: Blunting of the costophrenic sulcus with a homogeneous dependent opacity forming a concave upward meniscus along the lateral chest wall on upright views.
diseases.differential: Pleural thickening, basilar atelectasis, elevated hemidiaphragm, and loculated empyema or hemothorax.
diseases.followup: Point-of-care thoracic ultrasound is recommended to confirm free versus loculated fluid and guide diagnostic thoracentesis when clinically indicated per BTS Pleural Disease guidance.

diseases.hallmarks: Non-specific parenchymal opacity (deprecated as a standalone descriptor by Fleischner Society in favor of specific morphology such as ground-glass opacity or consolidation).
diseases.differential: Community-acquired pneumonia, cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, pulmonary hemorrhage, aspiration, and focal atelectasis.
diseases.followup: Describe exact zonal distribution and correlate with fever, leukocytosis, and prior films; consider chest CT when opacity persists or morphology remains indeterminate.

diseases.hallmarks: Rounded or lobulated focal parenchymal opacity measuring > 30 mm in diameter; plain chest radiography cannot definitively distinguish benign from malignant etiology.
diseases.differential: Primary bronchogenic carcinoma, solitary metastasis, round pneumonia, lung abscess, granuloma, and superimposed extrapulmonary structure.
diseases.followup: Dedicated contrast-enhanced chest CT is recommended for morphological characterization, staging, and multidisciplinary tissue sampling assessment.

diseases.hallmarks: Well- or poorly-defined rounded focal opacity measuring <= 30 mm in diameter surrounded by aerated lung parenchyma; must exclude nipple shadow or rib osteophyte overlap.
diseases.differential: Calcified granuloma, primary lung neoplasm, metastatic nodule, hamartoma, nipple shadow, and cutaneous lesion.
diseases.followup: Compare with historical radiographs to assess temporal stability; perform thin-section chest CT to confirm true parenchymal location and apply Fleischner nodule risk stratification.

diseases.hallmarks: Airspace consolidation or patchy parenchymal opacity, frequently with air bronchograms and silhouette sign obscuring adjacent cardiac or diaphragmatic borders.
diseases.differential: Pulmonary edema, alveolar hemorrhage, pulmonary infarction, organizing pneumonia, and atelectasis.
diseases.followup: Correlate with clinical severity scores, inflammatory biomarkers, and microbiology per local protocol; consider follow-up radiography in high-risk adults to document radiographic resolution.

diseases.hallmarks: Thin sharp white visceral pleural line displaced away from the chest wall with complete absence of peripheral bronchovascular markings beyond the line.
diseases.differential: Skin fold artifact (vessels continue beyond the edge), giant emphysematous bulla, pneumomediastinum, and medial scapular border.
diseases.followup: Immediate emergency clinical assessment if dyspnea, hypoxia, or hemodynamic instability (tension physiology) is present; physician determines observation, aspiration, or chest drain placement per BTS guidance.

diseases.hallmarks: Homogeneous increase in pulmonary parenchymal attenuation that obscures underlying vessels and airway walls, often containing patent air bronchograms without major volume loss.
diseases.differential: Infectious pneumonia, cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic edema, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, mucinous adenocarcinoma, and aspiration.
diseases.followup: Consolidation is a radiographic pattern rather than a final etiology; correlate with clinical history, laboratory markers, and prior studies to narrow infectious versus non-infectious causes.

diseases.hallmarks: Bilateral perihilar airspace opacities (bat-wing distribution), upper-lobe pulmonary venous cephalization, peribronchial cuffing, Kerley B septal lines, and often bilateral pleural effusions.
diseases.differential: Atypical or viral pneumonia, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and lymphangitic carcinomatosis.
diseases.followup: Prompt cardiopulmonary assessment including oxygen saturation, volume status, and cardiac biomarkers; acute hypoxemic respiratory distress requires urgent stabilization.

diseases.hallmarks: Bilateral pulmonary hyperlucency with attenuated peripheral vascular markings, flattened low-lying hemidiaphragms, widened retrosternal airspace, and possible focal bullae.
diseases.differential: Over-penetrated exposure technique, acute asthma hyperinflation, unilateral Swyer-James syndrome, and large pneumothorax.
diseases.followup: Correlate with smoking history and spirometry (FEV1/FVC) for COPD diagnosis; chest CT is reserved for surgical/bronchoscopic lung volume reduction or bullous disease evaluation.

diseases.hallmarks: Coarse reticular or reticulonodular opacities, architectural distortion, traction bronchiectasis, and basal or upper-zone volume loss suggesting chronic fibrotic remodeling.
diseases.differential: Interstitial pulmonary edema, post-infectious scarring (including prior tuberculosis), asbestosis, and lymphangitic tumor spread.
diseases.followup: Refer for pulmonology evaluation; high-resolution chest CT (HRCT) and pulmonary function tests (including DLCO) are recommended to classify interstitial lung disease subtype.

diseases.hallmarks: Focal or diffuse soft-tissue thickening along the parietal or visceral pleura (commonly apical capping or lateral chest wall), occasionally accompanied by pleural calcification.
diseases.differential: Loculated pleural effusion, extrapleural fat pad, asbestos-related pleural plaques, and pleural neoplasm (mesothelioma or metastasis).
diseases.followup: Review occupational asbestos exposure, prior empyema/tuberculosis history, and historical radiographs; obtain contrast-enhanced chest CT if nodular, circumferential, or progressive.

diseases.hallmarks: Retrocardiac radiolucent gas bubble or air-fluid level projecting behind the cardiac silhouette above the diaphragmatic contour, characteristic of hiatal or diaphragmatic herniation.
diseases.differential: Posterior mediastinal mass, esophageal achalasia, lower-lobe lung abscess, and eventration of the hemidiaphragm.
diseases.followup: Confirm anatomical hernia subtype and correlate with reflux or obstructive symptoms; consider chest/abdominal CT or upper gastrointestinal endoscopy if complicated.

diseases.hallmarks: Upper-lobe or superior-segment fibronodular opacities, parenchymal cavitation, hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, or miliary micronodules; radiographic appearance is suggestive but not bacteriologically specific.
diseases.differential: Non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection, necrotizing bacterial pneumonia, fungal cavitation (aspergillosis), lung malignancy, and sarcoidosis.
diseases.followup: Positive chest X-ray triage requires clinical assessment and WHO-recommended rapid molecular sputum testing (mWRD such as Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra), with AFB smear and culture as indicated.

diseases.hallmarks: Bilateral peripheral and lower-zone predominant hazy ground-glass opacities or consolidation; chest radiography is non-specific and cannot confirm SARS-CoV-2 infection.
diseases.differential: Other viral pneumonias (influenza, RSV), bacterial atypical pneumonia, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and cryptogenic organizing pneumonia.
diseases.followup: Perform viral confirmation testing (RT-PCR or antigen assay per local guidance), evaluate pulse oximetry and clinical risk factors, and audit Grad-CAM in-lung energy (>= 80%) to exclude shortcut artifacts.
